sla_notes_intro: The Bible is the collection of sacred writings that Christians regard as the inspired word of God, and Bible Knowledge is the study of its contents, message and teachings.
sla_notes_details: The word Bible comes from the Greek word biblia meaning books, because it is a library of 66 books (in the Protestant canon) written by many authors over about 1,500 years. Christians believe that the writers were inspired by the Holy Spirit (2 Timothy 3:16). The Bible is divided into the Old Testament, which records God's dealings with Israel before Christ, and the New Testament, which records the life and teaching of Jesus and the early Church. Bible Knowledge is a school subject that helps learners understand biblical stories, teachings and values and apply them to moral and social life.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student reading Psalm 119:105, 'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path', learns that the Bible is a guide for daily decisions.
sla_notes_daily_life: People use the Bible in worship, family prayers, counselling and moral education to decide between right and wrong.
sla_exercise: What does the word Bible mean?::It means books (from the Greek word biblia).||Name the two major divisions of the Bible.::The Old Testament and the New Testament.||Why is Bible Knowledge taught in schools?::To help learners understand biblical teaching and apply its moral values in life.

sla_notes_intro: The books of the Bible are grouped according to their type of writing and their position in the Old or New Testament.
sla_notes_details: The Old Testament has 39 books: the Law or Pentateuch (Genesis to Deuteronomy), the historical books (Joshua to Esther), the poetic or wisdom books (Job to Song of Solomon) and the prophetic books, which are divided into major prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel) and minor prophets (Hosea to Malachi). The New Testament has 27 books: the four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), the historical book of Acts, the Epistles or letters (Romans to Jude) and the prophetic book of Revelation. Knowing the classification helps a reader locate books quickly and understand their purpose.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Genesis belongs to the Pentateuch, Psalms belongs to the poetic books, Isaiah belongs to the major prophets and Luke belongs to the Gospels.
sla_notes_daily_life: Pastors and readers use this classification to find passages quickly during sermons, Sunday school and personal reading.
sla_exercise: How many books are in the Old Testament and the New Testament?::The Old Testament has 39 books and the New Testament has 27 books.||Name the first five books of the Bible.::Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy.||Under which group of books is the Gospel of Luke classified?::Under the Gospels of the New Testament.

sla_notes_intro: Genesis is the first book of the Bible and the book of beginnings, telling of the origin of the world, humankind, sin and the chosen people.
sla_notes_details: The name Genesis means origin or beginning. Tradition attributes its authorship to Moses. The book has two main parts: chapters 1 to 11, the primeval history covering creation, the fall, the flood and the tower of Babel; and chapters 12 to 50, the patriarchal history of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. Its main themes are God as creator, the dignity of human beings, sin and its consequences, God's covenant and promise, and God's providence. It was written to show Israel who God is and who they are as His people.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Genesis 1:1 says, 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth', which introduces God as creator of everything.
sla_notes_daily_life: The book of Genesis helps people answer questions about the origin of life, family, work and rest, which are important in everyday belief.
sla_exercise: What does the name Genesis mean?::Origin or beginning.||Who is traditionally believed to be the author of Genesis?::Moses.||Name two main themes of Genesis.::God as creator and the covenant promise (or sin and its consequences).

sla_notes_intro: God's creation is the belief that God made the universe, its living and non-living things, and human beings by His word and power.
sla_notes_details: Genesis 1:1 to 2:3 describes creation in six days with rest on the seventh: light, sky, land and plants, sun, moon and stars, sea creatures and birds, land animals and human beings. Genesis 2 gives a second account emphasising the making of man from dust and woman from his rib. Human beings were created in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), given a place in the Garden of Eden and blessed. The creation is described as good, showing the orderliness and purposefulness of God's work. The Sabbath was set apart as a day of rest and worship.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, on the sixth day God created man and woman and said everything He made was very good (Genesis 1:31).
sla_notes_daily_life: Believers thank God for life, food, rain and nature, and many communities set aside a day of rest and worship each week.
sla_exercise: On which day did God create human beings?::On the sixth day.||In whose image were human beings created?::In the image of God.||Which day did God bless and set apart as a day of rest?::The seventh day (the Sabbath).

sla_notes_intro: Human beings were given the duty to look after, use wisely and protect everything God created.
sla_notes_details: According to Genesis 1:28 and 2:15, God blessed man and told him to be fruitful, fill the earth, subdue it and rule over fish, birds and animals, and He placed him in the garden to work and take care of it. This makes man a steward, not an owner, who must use resources responsibly. Responsibilities include tilling the land, protecting plants and animals, naming and caring for animals, avoiding pollution and deforestation, and sharing resources. Living things such as plants and animals and non-living things such as water, soil and air depend on each other.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, students who plant trees, avoid littering and keep water sources clean are fulfilling the responsibility given to Adam to work and take care of the garden.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers who use soil conservation and communities that protect forests and rivers show care for God's creation.

sla_notes_intro: Life and the environment are gifts from God, so believers must protect and respect them.
sla_notes_details: The Bible teaches that life is sacred because human beings bear God's image, and the commandment 'You shall not kill' protects it. Caring for life includes avoiding violence and abortion, providing food, shelter and health care, and caring for the weak. Caring for the environment includes avoiding bush fires and littering, conserving soil and water, planting trees, and using resources wisely for future generations. Neglecting them leads to hunger, disease, floods and drought, which affect all people.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a school environmental club that plants trees around the compound and collects waste demonstrates the biblical duty to care for life and environment.
sla_notes_daily_life: Communities join clean-up days, tree planting and health campaigns to protect life and the surroundings.

sla_notes_intro: The Fall is the disobedience of Adam and Eve to God's command, which brought sin and death into the world.
sla_notes_details: In Genesis 3, God had allowed Adam and Eve to eat from every tree in Eden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The serpent tempted Eve, she ate and gave to Adam, and both disobeyed God. The consequences were shame and hiding, the curse on the serpent, pain in childbirth for the woman, hard labour and thorny ground for the man, broken relationship with God, expulsion from the garden and physical death. The narrative also shows God's mercy: He made garments of skin for them and promised a future victory over evil (Genesis 3:15). Cain's murder of Abel (Genesis 4) shows how sin spread.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when Adam blamed Eve and Eve blamed the serpent (Genesis 3:12-13), it shows that people often avoid taking responsibility for their mistakes.
sla_notes_daily_life: Temptation to disobey rules, lie or steal is part of daily life, and the story teaches people to resist and to take responsibility.

sla_notes_intro: The Patriarchs are the ancestors of Israel: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, through whom God worked out His covenant promise.
sla_notes_details: Abraham was called from Ur to Canaan (Genesis 12), promised land, descendants and blessing, and showed faith when he was ready to sacrifice Isaac (Genesis 22). Isaac, the son of promise, married Rebekah and had twins Esau and Jacob. Jacob deceived Esau, fled to Haran, wrestled with God and was renamed Israel; his twelve sons became the twelve tribes. Joseph, sold by his brothers to Egypt, rose to become governor, saved Egypt and his family from famine and forgave his brothers (Genesis 37-50). The lives of the Patriarchs teach faith, obedience, patience, forgiveness and trust in God's providence.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Joseph told his brothers, 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good' (Genesis 50:20), showing forgiveness.
sla_notes_daily_life: Families today can learn from the Patriarchs about faith, hard work, family reconciliation and leadership.

sla_notes_intro: Exodus is the second book of the Bible and tells how God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt and formed them into a nation.
sla_notes_details: The word Exodus means going out or departure. The book is traditionally attributed to Moses. Its main sections are Israel's oppression in Egypt (chapters 1-2), the call of Moses and the ten plagues (3-12), the Passover and crossing of the Red Sea (12-15), the journey in the wilderness (15-18), the giving of the law and covenant at Mount Sinai (19-24) and instructions for the tabernacle (25-40). Major themes are liberation, God's presence, covenant, law and worship.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, at the Red Sea God parted the waters so the Israelites crossed on dry land while Pharaoh's army was destroyed (Exodus 14).
sla_notes_daily_life: Exodus reminds believers that God hears the cry of the oppressed, encouraging people to fight injustice and support those in difficulty.
sla_exercise: What does Exodus mean?::Going out or departure.||Which feast commemorates the deliverance of Israel from Egypt?::The Passover.||Where did God give the law to Moses?::On Mount Sinai.

sla_notes_intro: God's love and compassion are shown in His care for the suffering Israelites and in His acts of rescue and provision.
sla_notes_details: God saw the affliction of His people, heard their cry and remembered His covenant (Exodus 2:23-25; 3:7-8). He called Moses to lead them, sent plagues on Egypt, protected Israel at the Passover, opened the Red Sea, guided them by a pillar of cloud and fire, and provided manna, quails and water in the wilderness. He also forgave them after the golden calf (Exodus 34:6, 'The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love'). Believers are called to imitate this love by showing compassion to others.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, God gave manna each morning (Exodus 16) so that the Israelites did not starve in the desert.
sla_notes_daily_life: People show God's love today by feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and helping orphans and widows.
sla_exercise: Which food did God provide for Israel in the wilderness?::Manna and quails.||Which verse describes God as merciful and gracious?::Exodus 34:6.||Give one way people can show compassion today.::Feeding the hungry or helping the sick and needy.

sla_notes_intro: Failure to appreciate God's love and compassion leads to complaining, disobedience, idolatry and punishment.
sla_notes_details: After their rescue the Israelites grumbled about water and food (Exodus 15-17), tried to keep manna overnight against instruction, worshipped the golden calf while Moses was on Sinai (Exodus 32), and later refused to trust God. The consequences included hunger and thirst, plagues, the death of many, the breaking of the tablets, loss of fellowship with God and a wandering that lasted forty years. Ingratitude also damages relationships between people. Gratitude, obedience and worship are the proper responses.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when the people made the golden calf, about three thousand died and God's presence was withdrawn for a time (Exodus 32:28, 33:3).
sla_notes_daily_life: Ungrateful behaviour today, such as wasting food or disrespecting parents and teachers, leads to broken relationships and loss of blessings.

sla_notes_intro: The Sinai Covenant is the agreement made between God and Israel at Mount Sinai in which God promised to be their God and they promised to obey His law.
sla_notes_details: In Exodus 19-24 God brought Israel to Sinai and said that if they obeyed His voice and kept His covenant they would be His treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people agreed ('All that the Lord has spoken we will do'). God gave the Ten Commandments and other laws, and the covenant was sealed with the sacrifice of animals and the sprinkling of blood. Features of the covenant are: initiative by God, conditions of obedience, promises of blessing, and a sign of sealing. It made Israel a community set apart for God's service.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Exodus 24:3-8 Moses read the Book of the Covenant to the people, they promised obedience, and he sprinkled blood on the altar and people as a seal.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern agreements such as marriage vows, contracts and school rules also involve promises and obligations, just as the covenant did.
sla_exercise: Where was the covenant between God and Israel made?::At Mount Sinai.||What did Israel promise to do?::To obey all that God commanded.||How was the covenant sealed?::By animal sacrifice and the sprinkling of blood.

sla_notes_intro: The Ten Commandments in Exodus 20 are the basic laws God gave Israel governing worship of God and relationships with people.
sla_notes_details: The first four commandments concern duty to God: have no other gods, make no idols, do not take the Lord's name in vain, and keep the Sabbath holy. The last six concern duty to neighbour: honour father and mother, do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, and do not covet. They were written on two tablets of stone. They promote love of God, justice, family stability, honesty and peace. Jesus later summarised them as love for God and love for neighbour.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, obeying the eighth commandment means not stealing school property, and obeying the ninth means telling the truth in class and in court.
sla_notes_daily_life: The commandments guide behaviour in families, workplaces and society by discouraging theft, violence, lies and disrespect.

sla_notes_intro: Moses was the leader God used to deliver Israel, and his life shows qualities of a good leader.
sla_notes_details: Moses showed obedience to God's call despite fear (Exodus 3-4), courage in facing Pharaoh, humility (Numbers 12:3), intercession for the people (Exodus 32:11-14), patience with a complaining nation, wisdom in accepting the advice of Jethro to delegate judges (Exodus 18), faithfulness in teaching the law, and dependence on God through prayer. These qualities enabled him to lead over a million people through the wilderness. Leaders today are expected to be responsible, accountable and servant-hearted.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when Jethro advised him to appoint able men as judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, Moses accepted and shared the workload.
sla_notes_daily_life: Class monitors, prefects, and community and national leaders can copy Moses by being humble, listening to advice and serving others.

sla_notes_intro: Statistics is the collection, counting and organising of information about people or things, and the Book of Numbers records two censuses of Israel.
sla_notes_details: The book is called Numbers because it records the counting of the people, first at Sinai (Numbers 1) and later on the plains of Moab (Numbers 26). Only men aged twenty and above who could go to war were counted, and the Levites were counted separately (Numbers 3-4) from one month old. The tribes were numbered and arranged around the tabernacle. The census gave the total of about 603,550 fighting men in the first count. Statistics in the Bible show that God is a God of order and that planning requires accurate information.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the first census in Numbers 1 listed the number of men able to fight in each tribe, such as Judah with 74,600.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern statistics appear in population census, school enrolment records, health data and election registers.
sla_exercise: Why is the fourth book of the Bible called Numbers?::Because it records the counting (census) of the Israelites.||Who were counted separately from the other tribes?::The Levites.||Give one modern example of statistics.::The national population census.

sla_notes_intro: A census is an official counting of the population, and it gives information used for planning and administration.
sla_notes_details: In Numbers the census was used to organise the army, arrange the camp, allocate work to the Levites and later share the land among the tribes (Numbers 26:52-56). Today the objectives of a census are to know the size and composition of the population, to plan services such as education, health, roads and water, to allocate resources and constituencies, to monitor development and to prepare for emergencies. Statistics help government, organisations and families make informed decisions. Accurate and honest reporting is essential, and citizens should co-operate with census officers.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a census showing many school-age children in a district helps the government decide where to build more classrooms.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tanzania conducts a national census every ten years, and households give correct information to enumerators.

sla_notes_intro: Joshua records how Israel, under Joshua's leadership, entered, conquered and settled the Promised Land of Canaan.
sla_notes_details: The book is named after Joshua, the successor of Moses. Its main ideas are: the commissioning of Joshua and God's promise to be with him (chapter 1); the crossing of the Jordan (3-4); the fall of Jericho and Ai (6-8); the conquest of southern and northern Canaan (9-12); the division of the land among the tribes (13-21); and Joshua's farewell speech and covenant renewal at Shechem (23-24). Themes include obedience, courage, God's faithfulness, holiness and the danger of disobedience as shown in Achan's sin.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, God told Joshua, 'Be strong and courageous... for the Lord your God is with you wherever you go' (Joshua 1:9).
sla_notes_daily_life: Believers draw courage from Joshua when facing exams, challenges or leadership responsibilities.
sla_exercise: Whom did Joshua succeed as leader of Israel?::Moses.||Name one main event in the Book of Joshua.::The crossing of the Jordan (or the fall of Jericho, or the division of the land).||Which verse tells Joshua to be strong and courageous?::Joshua 1:9.

sla_notes_intro: Leaders must be prepared and trained before taking responsibility, as shown by the preparation of Joshua.
sla_notes_details: Joshua was trained under Moses as a servant, a military commander (Exodus 17), a spy sent to Canaan (Numbers 13-14) and a companion on Sinai. Moses laid hands on him publicly (Numbers 27:18-23; Deuteronomy 34:9), and God directly commissioned him and promised His presence. Preparing leaders ensures continuity, stability, wisdom, discipline and a smooth transfer of authority, and it prevents conflict and confusion. Preparation includes mentoring, training, giving responsibility and moral formation.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Joshua served for many years as Moses' assistant before leading Israel, so the people accepted him when Moses died.
sla_notes_daily_life: Schools, churches and companies prepare leaders through prefect training, deputy roles and mentoring programmes.

sla_notes_intro: Jericho fell by God's power through obedience to His instructions, while Ai defeated Israel first because of Achan's sin.
sla_notes_details: In Joshua 6 the Israelites marched around Jericho once a day for six days and seven times on the seventh day with priests blowing trumpets; at the shout the walls collapsed and the city was destroyed, and only Rahab and her family were spared. In Joshua 7 Israel was defeated at Ai because Achan took forbidden goods from Jericho; after he was punished, God gave Israel victory by an ambush (Joshua 8). The lessons are that victory comes by faith and obedience, and that the sin of one person can affect the whole community.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Rahab was saved because she hid the two spies and had faith in the God of Israel (Joshua 2, 6:25).
sla_notes_daily_life: Cheating or corruption by one member of a group can bring trouble to all, while obedience and faith bring success.
sla_exercise: How many days did Israel march around Jericho?::Seven days.||Why did Israel lose the first battle at Ai?::Because Achan had taken forbidden goods from Jericho.||Who was saved when Jericho fell?::Rahab and her family.

sla_notes_intro: Strength and bravery are the courage and determination to do what is right despite danger, as shown by Joshua, Caleb and others.
sla_notes_details: God repeatedly told Joshua to be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:6-9). Indicators of bravery include crossing the Jordan at flood stage, marching against fortified cities, Caleb's request for the hill country at age eighty-five (Joshua 14:10-12), Rahab's risk in hiding the spies, and the people's readiness to obey. Real strength depends on trust in God, knowledge of His word and obedience, and not merely on military power.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Caleb said, 'I am as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me' (Joshua 14:11), showing determination in old age.
sla_notes_daily_life: Students show bravery when they refuse peer pressure, report wrongdoing or attempt difficult tasks.
sla_exercise: Who asked for the hill country at the age of eighty-five?::Caleb.||Which verse tells Joshua to be strong and courageous?::Joshua 1:9.||On what does real strength depend according to Joshua?::On trust in God and obedience to His word.

sla_notes_intro: Bravery, humility and perseverance are virtues that enabled Israel's leaders to complete the task of possessing the land.
sla_notes_details: Bravery was shown in confronting enemies; humility in Joshua's submission to God (falling on his face before the commander of the Lord's army, Joshua 5:14) and in the acceptance of God's instructions without questioning; perseverance in the years of war lasting about seven years and the patient marching around Jericho for seven days. These virtues bring success, unity and honour, and their absence leads to failure as in the defeat at Ai. Believers are encouraged to keep trying even when the task is long and hard.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Israel continued to march around Jericho silently for six days before the walls fell on the seventh.
sla_notes_daily_life: A student who studies patiently for years and remains humble in success demonstrates these qualities.
sla_exercise: Give one example of humility from Joshua.::Joshua fell on his face and worshipped before the commander of the Lord's army.||Which event shows perseverance?::The seven days of marching around Jericho (or the years of conquest).||What can result from lack of humility and obedience?::Failure and defeat, as at Ai.

sla_notes_intro: Patriotism is love for and loyalty to one's country and readiness to defend and develop it.
sla_notes_details: In Joshua, the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh crossed the Jordan to help fight for the land even though their own inheritance was already east of the river (Joshua 1:12-18; 22). The people obeyed Joshua, fought for the land and settled it according to allotment. Rahab's loyalty later shifted to Israel's God. Patriotic behaviour includes obeying laws, paying taxes, defending the nation, working hard, protecting national resources, keeping peace and avoiding corruption.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the eastern tribes told Joshua, 'All that you have commanded us we will do' and joined their brothers in the war.
sla_notes_daily_life: Citizens show patriotism by participating in national events, voting, paying taxes, protecting public property and speaking well of their country.
sla_exercise: Define patriotism.::Love for and loyalty to one's country, with readiness to serve and defend it.||Which tribes helped in the conquest though they already had land east of the Jordan?::Reuben, Gad and half of the tribe of Manasseh.||State one way a student can show patriotism.::By obeying laws and protecting public property.

sla_notes_intro: The word Gospel means good news, and the Gospels are the four New Testament books telling the good news of Jesus Christ, which was set in the context of Jewish religious institutions.
sla_notes_details: The English word Gospel comes from the Old English godspel meaning good news, translating the Greek euangelion. The four Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; the first three are called Synoptic because they see events in a similar way. Jewish institutions in the time of Jesus include the Temple in Jerusalem, the synagogue as a place of prayer and teaching on the Sabbath, the Sanhedrin as the highest council and court, the priesthood, the scribes who interpreted the law, the Pharisees and Sadducees as religious groups, and festivals such as Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles. Understanding them helps readers understand the settings and conflicts in Luke.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Luke 4:16-21 Jesus read the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth on the Sabbath, showing the role of the synagogue.
sla_notes_daily_life: Today places of worship, religious councils and religious festivals play roles similar to Jewish institutions in guiding believers.
sla_exercise: What does the word Gospel mean?::Good news.||Name the Synoptic Gospels.::Matthew, Mark and Luke.||Which Jewish institution was the highest council and court?::The Sanhedrin.

sla_notes_intro: The Gospel according to Luke was written by Luke, a physician and companion of Paul, to Theophilus and to Gentile readers.
sla_notes_details: Author: Luke is described by Paul as the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), a Gentile Christian, and also the writer of the Acts of the Apostles. Recipients: the Gospel is addressed to Theophilus, meaning lover of God (Luke 1:3), representing Gentile Christians in general. Purpose: Luke wrote an orderly account so that the reader might know the certainty of the things taught (Luke 1:1-4), to show that salvation is for all people, and to present Jesus as the Saviour and perfect Son of Man. Luke stresses Jesus' concern for the poor, women, outcasts and sinners, and he researched eyewitness accounts.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Luke 1:3 says 'it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you'.
sla_notes_daily_life: Careful research and honest reporting, as done by Luke, are important in journalism, education and courts of law today.
sla_exercise: Who wrote the Gospel according to Luke?::Luke, the physician and companion of Paul.||To whom was the Gospel addressed?::To Theophilus and Gentile readers.||State the purpose of writing the Gospel of Luke.::To give an orderly account so that readers know the truth about Jesus and that salvation is for all.

sla_notes_intro: Themes are the main teaching ideas running through the Gospel, and Luke emphasises salvation for all, the Holy Spirit, prayer, praise, women and the lost.
sla_notes_details: Salvation for all: Jesus came for Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor (Luke 2:10, 19:10). Work of the Holy Spirit: He is active in the conception of Jesus, at His baptism, in His temptation and ministry (Luke 1:35; 3:22; 4:1, 18). Worship and praise: songs such as the Magnificat and Benedictus and joy at Jesus' works. Role of women: Mary, Elizabeth, Anna, the widow of Nain, Martha and Mary and the women at the tomb. The Gospel of the lost: the parables of the lost sheep, coin and son (Luke 15). The Gospel of prayer: Jesus prays at baptism, before choosing apostles, at Gethsemane and on the cross, and teaches the Lord's Prayer (Luke 11:1-4).
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in the parable of the lost sheep the shepherd searches until he finds it and rejoices, showing that God seeks sinners.
sla_notes_daily_life: These themes encourage people today to pray, praise God, respect women and welcome the marginalised.
sla_exercise: Which chapter of Luke contains the parables of the lost sheep, lost coin and lost son?::Luke 15.||Name two themes in the Gospel of Luke.::Salvation for all and the role of women (or prayer, the Holy Spirit, worship and praise).||Which songs of praise appear in Luke 1-2?::The Magnificat and the Benedictus (also the Nunc Dimittis).

sla_notes_intro: Jesus used parables and miracles to teach about the Kingdom of God and to show His power and compassion.
sla_notes_details: A parable is an earthly story with a heavenly meaning drawn from everyday life; examples in Luke are the good Samaritan, the rich fool, the prodigal son, the persistent widow and the Pharisee and tax collector. Jesus used them to make teaching simple, to challenge listeners and to reveal truth to those willing to understand. A miracle is an extraordinary act showing God's power. Types in Luke include healing (the leper, the paralytic), nature miracles (calming the storm), casting out demons (the Gerasene demoniac) and raising the dead (the widow's son at Nain, Jairus' daughter). Miracles demonstrate compassion, authority and the arrival of God's Kingdom, and they call for faith.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37) teaches that our neighbour is anyone in need regardless of tribe or religion.
sla_notes_daily_life: Teachers still use stories and demonstrations to explain difficult ideas, and believers help the sick and needy as Jesus did.

sla_notes_intro: Human rights are the basic freedoms and entitlements of every person, and Luke shows Jesus defending the dignity and rights of the weak.
sla_notes_details: Luke shows Jesus proclaiming release to captives and freedom to the oppressed (Luke 4:18-19), healing on the Sabbath to restore dignity (13:10-17), accepting the poor, women, tax collectors, lepers and Samaritans, teaching justice in the parable of the persistent widow (18:1-8), defending the widow's offering, and commanding equal treatment (6:31). Rights supported include the right to life, health, equality, freedom from oppression, food, and care for the poor. Believers are called to speak out against exploitation, discrimination and abuse.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Jesus healed the crippled woman on the Sabbath and called her a daughter of Abraham, restoring her honour (Luke 13:10-17).
sla_notes_daily_life: Christians and others defend rights by helping abused children, opposing gender-based violence and supporting the poor and disabled.

sla_notes_intro: The teachings of Luke can be applied to solve everyday problems in family, school and society.
sla_notes_details: Each theme has a practical application. Salvation for all encourages acceptance of people from different backgrounds. The work of the Holy Spirit encourages guidance, courage and good character. Worship and praise call for thanks and regular prayer. The role of women encourages respect and equal opportunity. The Gospel of the lost calls for forgiving and helping those who have gone astray. The Gospel of prayer calls for persistent prayer and trust. A learner chooses one theme, gathers evidence from Luke, relates it to a real situation in the community, and prepares a report as course work to be submitted in Form Four.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a project on the theme of the lost could study how a community helps street children return to school, using the parable of the lost son.
sla_notes_daily_life: Applying biblical themes helps solve problems such as discrimination, family conflict and neglect of the needy.

sla_notes_intro: A family is a basic social group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together and support one another.
sla_notes_details: Types of families include nuclear (parents and children), extended (including relatives), single-parent and polygamous families. Functions are procreation, care and protection, socialisation and education of children, provision of basic needs, moral and religious training, and emotional support. The biblical basis is found in Genesis 2:24, where a man leaves his parents and is joined to his wife, and in the commandment to honour father and mother. Members have roles: parents provide and guide, and children obey and help.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Luke 2:41-52 the family of Joseph, Mary and Jesus travelled together to Jerusalem for the Passover, showing shared religious life.
sla_notes_daily_life: Families provide food, shelter, love and discipline and are the first school for every child.
sla_exercise: Define a family.::A basic social group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption who live together.||Name two functions of the family.::Provision of basic needs and moral/religious training of children.||Which verse in Genesis provides the biblical basis for marriage and family?::Genesis 2:24.

sla_notes_intro: Luke presents different families whose characteristics of faith, love, obedience and sometimes conflict teach lessons about family life.
sla_notes_details: The family of Zechariah and Elizabeth was righteous, prayerful and faithful, and they received a son, John, as an answer to prayer (Luke 1). The Holy Family of Joseph, Mary and Jesus was obedient to the law, worshipped together and raised Jesus in wisdom (Luke 2). Martha and Mary hosted Jesus, though they differed in priorities (10:38-42). The family of Jairus sought help for their sick daughter (8:40-56). The family in the parable of the prodigal son shows a father's forgiving love and the jealousy of an elder brother (15:11-32). Characteristics include love, hospitality, prayer, faith, obedience, forgiveness and shared responsibility.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Luke 2:51 Jesus went down with his parents to Nazareth and was obedient to them.
sla_notes_daily_life: Families today can copy these qualities by praying together, forgiving one another and sharing duties.

sla_notes_intro: Good parental care means providing for, protecting, teaching and lovingly guiding children until they mature.
sla_notes_details: Luke shows Mary and Joseph presenting Jesus at the temple, circumcising and naming Him, taking Him to Jerusalem yearly and searching anxiously when He was lost (Luke 2:21-52). Zechariah and Elizabeth raised John in the ways of God. The father in the prodigal son story gave freedom, waited patiently, forgave and welcomed his son. Jairus sought healing for his daughter. Good parental care includes provision of food and shelter, education, spiritual guidance, discipline with love, protection from harm, time together and being good role models.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, when Jesus was found in the temple, Mary said, 'Your father and I have been searching for you anxiously', showing parental concern.
sla_notes_daily_life: Parents show care by paying school fees, checking homework, giving advice and attending school meetings.

sla_notes_intro: The Acts of the Apostles was written by Luke as the second part of his work, telling of the growth of the early Church.
sla_notes_details: Author: Luke, the writer of the Third Gospel, as shown by the address to Theophilus and the similar style (Acts 1:1); he uses 'we' passages when travelling with Paul. Recipients: Theophilus and Gentile Christians. Purpose: to show how the Gospel spread from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8), to explain the work of the Holy Spirit, to show that salvation is for Jews and Gentiles, to defend Christianity as lawful and to give an orderly history of the early Church. It probably was written about AD 62-70.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Acts 1:1 begins 'In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach', linking it to Luke's Gospel.
sla_notes_daily_life: Historical records like Acts help us to know how our faith and institutions began and grew.

sla_notes_intro: The themes of Acts are the central ideas that show how the Church began and spread.
sla_notes_details: Major themes are the work of the Holy Spirit (Pentecost, Acts 2, guiding missionaries), the spread of the Gospel from Jerusalem to Rome, the universality of salvation for Jews and Gentiles (Cornelius, Acts 10), witnessing and preaching, prayer and worship, fellowship and sharing of goods (2:44-47), persecution and courage, healing miracles, and the unity of the Church. The Gospel is always presented as the fulfilment of Old Testament promises and as good news for all people.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, at Pentecost the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke in other tongues so that people of many nations heard the Gospel in their own languages (Acts 2).
sla_notes_daily_life: Today, churches continue to pray, share with the needy, live together in unity and witness through preaching and social service.
sla_exercise: Which event in Acts 2 marks the coming of the Holy Spirit?::The Day of Pentecost.||Name two themes of Acts.::The work of the Holy Spirit and the spread of the Gospel.||Which Gentile officer received the Gospel in Acts 10?::Cornelius.

sla_notes_intro: Acts shows the apostles and early Christians defending the rights of the weak and their own right to worship and speak freely.
sla_notes_details: Peter and John said, 'We must obey God rather than men' when told to stop preaching (Acts 4:19; 5:29), defending freedom of religion and speech. The Church cared for widows so that no one lacked (6:1-6) and shared possessions (4:32-35), upholding the right to food and support. Paul and Silas claimed their rights as Roman citizens after being beaten unlawfully in Philippi (16:37), and Paul appealed to Caesar for a fair trial (25:11). Peter accepted Gentiles, upholding equality (10:34-35). These examples encourage believers to fight discrimination, unfair treatment and violations of freedom.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Acts 6 the Hellenist widows were being neglected in the daily distribution, so seven men were appointed to make it fair.
sla_notes_daily_life: Citizens today defend rights by using courts, reporting abuse and standing up for freedom of worship and equal treatment.
sla_exercise: Which apostles said 'We must obey God rather than men'?::Peter and John.||How did Paul defend his rights in Philippi?::He claimed his Roman citizenship after being beaten without trial.||Which problem in Acts 6 involved the rights of widows?::The neglect of Greek-speaking widows in the daily distribution of food.

sla_notes_intro: The Great Commission is Jesus' command to His disciples to spread the Gospel to all nations.
sla_notes_details: In Acts 1:8 Jesus said, 'You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.' The order of spread was therefore Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and the wider world. The disciples were told to wait for the Spirit, then witness by preaching, teaching, baptising and living the faith. The Gospel spread through Peter and John, Philip to Samaria and Ethiopia, and Paul to Asia Minor, Greece and Rome. The commission continues to every believer.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Philip preached to the Samaritans and explained the scriptures to the Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza (Acts 8).
sla_notes_daily_life: Believers spread the Gospel today through preaching, Sunday school, radio, social media and community service.
sla_exercise: Which verse contains the order to witness in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the end of the earth?::Acts 1:8.||Who preached to the Ethiopian official?::Philip.||What must disciples receive before witnessing?::Power of the Holy Spirit.

sla_notes_intro: The Holy Spirit gave power, guidance and unity to the early Church so that the Gospel could spread.
sla_notes_details: At Pentecost the Spirit came as wind and fire and enabled the apostles to preach boldly, and 3,000 people were baptised (Acts 2). The Spirit guided missionary work: He told Philip to go to the Ethiopian, told Peter to go to Cornelius, and set apart Barnabas and Saul at Antioch (13:2). He empowered miracles, gave courage in persecution, appointed leaders, and gave spiritual gifts for building up the Church. Without the Spirit the disciples were fearful; with Him they became bold witnesses.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after receiving the Spirit, Peter, who had denied Jesus, boldly preached to the crowd in Jerusalem.
sla_notes_daily_life: Believers pray for guidance and courage before big tasks, trusting the Holy Spirit as their helper.
sla_exercise: What happened on the day of Pentecost?::The Holy Spirit came upon the disciples and they spoke in other languages.||Which two men did the Spirit set apart at Antioch?::Barnabas and Saul.||State one role of the Holy Spirit in the early Church.::He gave power and courage to preach (or guided the missionaries).

sla_notes_intro: The early Christian community lived in fellowship, sharing and worship, and this life attracted many people to the faith.
sla_notes_details: Acts 2:42-47 and 4:32-35 describe believers devoting themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayer. They met daily in the temple and homes, sold property and shared with those in need so that no one lacked, worshipped with gladness and had favour with all people. They suffered persecution but stayed united. Their life-style acted as a witness, and the Lord added to their number daily. Leaders included the apostles and later deacons and elders.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Barnabas sold a field and gave the money to the apostles to help the needy (Acts 4:36-37).
sla_notes_daily_life: Communities today copy this by sharing food, contributing to funds for the needy and supporting one another in joy and sorrow.

sla_notes_intro: Courage is boldness to stand for the faith despite danger, and the apostles displayed it repeatedly.
sla_notes_details: Peter and John preached before the Sanhedrin after being arrested and said they could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard (Acts 4). The apostles rejoiced after being beaten (5:41). Stephen preached boldly and became the first martyr (7). Philip went to the despised Samaritans. Paul faced beatings, imprisonment, shipwreck and stoning yet continued (14:19-20; 27). Ananias obeyed God and visited Saul, the persecutor. Courage came from the Holy Spirit, prayer and conviction.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Stephen prayed for those stoning him, 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them' (Acts 7:60).
sla_notes_daily_life: Students show courage by standing for truth, refusing bad company and reporting wrongdoing.
sla_exercise: Who was the first Christian martyr?::Stephen.||Give two examples of courage shown by the apostles.::Peter and John preaching before the Sanhedrin and rejoicing after being beaten.||What was the source of the apostles' courage?::The Holy Spirit and their faith in Christ.

sla_notes_intro: Saul, a persecutor of the Church, met the risen Christ on the road to Damascus, became Paul and led missionary journeys to spread the Gospel.
sla_notes_details: Saul approved of Stephen's death and persecuted Christians (Acts 8:1-3). On the way to Damascus a bright light shone, he heard Jesus say, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?', was blinded and was later healed and baptised by Ananias (Acts 9). He preached in Damascus and Jerusalem. First journey (Acts 13-14) with Barnabas: Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Second journey (15:36-18:22) with Silas: Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth. Third journey (18:23-21:17): Ephesus, then back to Jerusalem. He was arrested, appealed to Caesar and was taken to Rome (Acts 21-28).
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Philippi Paul and Silas sang in prison, an earthquake opened the doors, and the jailer and his household believed (Acts 16).
sla_notes_daily_life: Paul's change from persecutor to preacher shows that people can change, and it encourages perseverance in service.
sla_exercise: On which road did Saul meet Jesus?::The road to Damascus.||Who baptised Saul in Damascus?::Ananias.||Name two cities Paul visited on the second missionary journey.::Philippi and Corinth (also Thessalonica or Athens).

sla_notes_intro: As the Church grew, conflicts arose, and the apostles resolved them through prayer, dialogue and wise leadership.
sla_notes_details: Examples of conflict are the complaint of Hellenist widows about neglect (Acts 6), the deceit of Ananias and Sapphira (5), disputes about whether Gentiles must be circumcised (15), and the quarrel between Paul and Barnabas over John Mark (15:36-40). Resolutions included appointing seven deacons for fair distribution, dealing firmly with dishonesty, and calling the Jerusalem Council for discussion and a common decision. Methods were prayer, listening to all sides, referring to scripture, delegating authority and seeking the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the twelve called the disciples together and had the community choose seven men to serve tables, which ended the widows' complaint.
sla_notes_daily_life: Schools, families and communities settle conflicts through dialogue, mediation and fair leadership.
sla_exercise: How was the widows' dispute in Acts 6 resolved?::Seven deacons were appointed to serve in the daily distribution.||Name one conflict in the early Church.::The dispute about circumcision of Gentile converts (or the deceit of Ananias and Sapphira).||State one method used to solve conflicts in the early Church.::Dialogue and prayerful discussion (the Jerusalem Council).

sla_notes_intro: Deacons are servants of the Church chosen to assist the apostles with practical duties so that the apostles could focus on prayer and the word.
sla_notes_details: In Acts 6:1-6 seven men were appointed, including Stephen and Philip. Reasons: the apostles were overloaded, and the needy widows were being neglected. Functions: serving tables, distributing food and aid, helping the needy, and also preaching (Stephen, Philip). Qualities: of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom (Acts 6:3), faithful, honest, hard-working and compassionate. The apostles prayed and laid hands on them. Their appointment improved administration and sped the growth of the Church.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, Philip the deacon preached in Samaria and baptised the Ethiopian official (Acts 8).
sla_notes_daily_life: Church committees, school prefects and community workers help leaders by taking up specific responsibilities.
sla_exercise: How many deacons were chosen in Acts 6?::Seven.||State two qualities required of deacons.::Good reputation and being full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom.||Give one function of the deacons.::To distribute food and help the needy so the apostles could pray and preach.

sla_notes_intro: The Jerusalem Council was a meeting of apostles and elders around AD 49 that settled whether Gentile believers must keep the Jewish law of circumcision.
sla_notes_details: Some Jewish Christians from Judea insisted that Gentiles be circumcised to be saved (Acts 15:1). Paul and Barnabas went to Jerusalem where Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James spoke. Peter said God gives the Spirit to Gentiles and that salvation is by grace; Paul and Barnabas reported the signs among the Gentiles; James quoted scripture and proposed that Gentiles should not be burdened but should avoid idols, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. The decision was written in a letter and carried to Antioch by Judas and Silas. The methods used were open debate, testimony, scriptural evidence, agreement and clear communication, and they brought peace, equality and unity.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, James said 'we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God', giving Gentiles equal acceptance.
sla_notes_daily_life: Modern councils, meetings and courts use open discussion and written decisions to bring peace and equality.
sla_exercise: Who presided over and gave the final proposal at the Jerusalem Council?::James.||What issue did the Council settle?::Whether Gentile converts had to be circumcised and follow the Jewish law.||State two methods used by the Council to solve the conflict.::Open discussion and appeal to testimony and scripture.
